articles.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline.
articles.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and "for many people, the high streets they grew up with have become unrecognisable".

BBC News has exposed organised crime on high streets across the country, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes and vapes, selling cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least £1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham said "the rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for".

He added: "That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do.

"We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on new government policies empowering local councils to regulate vape and betting shops, aiming to revitalize town centres and reduce crime linked to illegal sales and money laundering. This has broad societal significance by improving community well-being and local control, with clear substance and detailed measures described.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New government rules will help local councils control vape and betting shops to make UK town centres safer and more welcoming.

articles.title: 'I felt Tourette's would ruin my life, now I teach at Cambridge'
articles.summary: Amanda Cole previously hid her condition but now wants others to "tic freely" without embarrassment.
articles.content:
Dr Amanda Cole was 15 and sitting in a religious studies class when she experienced a peculiar spasm at the back of throat. She assumed it would pass, but it was a vocal tic and her first known manifestation of her Tourette's syndrome, a condition that causes people to make sudden, repetitive sounds or movements.

"How am I going to have a family? How am I going to have a job?" Cole, 32, remembers asking herself as she lay awake at night after her diagnosis in her 20s at her home on the Debden Estate near Loughton, Essex. "I thought it was going to destroy my life."

Now a married mother-of-one, Cole is an assistant professor in sociolinguistics at Cambridge University, but throughout her academic life she has kept her Tourette's hidden - until now.

Following an incident at this year's Bafta Film Awards ceremony in which a guest shouted out offensive words because of his tics, Cole said she wanted to be open about her condition and allowed the BBC to join her as she began telling colleagues and students.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights an inspiring personal story of overcoming stigma related to Tourette's syndrome, promoting acceptance and openness about neurological conditions. Amanda Cole's journey from fear of her diagnosis to becoming a Cambridge professor and advocate for tic freedom has broad societal significance in reducing stigma and encouraging inclusivity.
articles.personality_title: From hiding tics to teaching at Cambridge: Amanda Cole’s story
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Tourette’s syndrome is a condition that makes people have sudden, repeated movements or sounds called tics. Many who have it feel embarrassed or worried about how others will react.

**What happened** – Amanda Cole first noticed her vocal tic at age 15 but kept her condition secret for many years. After being diagnosed in her 20s, she feared it would stop her from having a normal life. Despite her worries, she became an assistant professor at Cambridge University. Recently, she started openly talking about her Tourette’s to help others feel less ashamed.

**Impact** – Amanda’s story shows it is possible to live a full and successful life with Tourette’s. By sharing her experience, she helps reduce the misunderstanding and stigma around the condition. This encourages others with tics to be more open and confident.

**What’s next step** – Amanda plans to continue speaking publicly about Tourette’s and support students and colleagues who have tics. Her openness may lead to more acceptance in schools and workplaces.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Amanda Cole’s journey from fear to openness teaches that Tourette’s does not have to limit your dreams or who you are.

articles.title: UN calls for urgent action to protect children from online information risks
articles.summary: More than eight in 10 young people aged 15 to 24 worldwide are now online, and in low-income countries they outpace the rest of the population nearly two to one.
articles.content:
The UN warned on Monday that this deeply connected generation too often bears the brunt of the risks to information integrity, including disinformation, harassment, algorithmic biases and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI).

In a new brief published ahead of International Youth Day, the UN urges Member States, technology companies, advertisers, media and researchers to prioritise protection and participation to address harms.

Tweet URL

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called last month for an AI Child Safety Pledge, comparing emerging AI technology to untested medicine as he urged stronger regulation.

“No child should be a guinea pig for unregulated AI…When a child is harmed, the answer must never be ‘the algorithm did it,” Mr. Guterres said in July at the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

Online harms no accident

The brief argues that the harms young people face online are not accidental. Rather, they are the product of business models that monetise attention and personal data, and of design choices built to maximise engagement and spending.

From algorithms that keep young users hooked to “dark patterns”, loot boxes and other tactics that drive compulsive use, the brief warns that children – whose habits, identities and relationships are still forming – are especially exposed.

AI, it adds, is outpacing efforts to respond to its rapid adoption, compounding risks such as AI-generated content to AI-facilitated exploitation.

It also identifies increasingly hidden advertising tactics as a means to exploit children to increase online spending.

“Taken together, these practices normalise pervasive commercial surveillance and manipulative design during the years when children and young people are most impressionable,” the brief reads.

Not only at risk

Children and youth are far more than potential victims, the brief stresses. They are creators, advocates and organizers, from youth-led movements reshaping civic life to young journalists and content creators contributing to public debate.

Yet the same online spaces that power youth movements also expose their organisers – often young women, minorities and activists – to online harassment and surveillance.

Young people’s perspectives must be integrated into research and policymaking that drives solutions to issues surrounding information integrity, the brief argues.

“Children and young people are among those most affected by today’s information crisis and among those most capable of helping to solve it,” said Charlotte Scaddan, UN Senior Adviser on Information Integrity. “Protecting them and including them are not competing goals. We have to do both.”

Window is closing fast

Governments and advocates have increasingly pushed children’s online safety to the forefront of policy debates on addictive design features, behavioural advertising, content moderation and privacy, the brief notes.

But with AI becoming increasingly ubiquitous, it warns the window is closing to write children’s rights into AI governance frameworks.

It suggests pathways for Member States to create laws, technology companies to protect child safety, advertisers to prioritise children’s rights, news media to serve young audiences and researchers to close gaps – such as in the Global South.

The UN continues to contribute to AI regulation efforts, including through the Global Dialogue and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – a scientific body to assess the opportunities and risks of AI.

“As digital technologies and information environments continue to evolve, the current moment presents an urgent opportunity to move from principles to practical action,” the brief says.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
articles.summary: Women can make higher returns but only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men.
articles.content:
It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm.

"Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says.

"Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."

Teleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."

When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?

One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a positive shift in women's financial empowerment and investment success, showing women can achieve higher returns and are increasingly participating in wealth creation. This represents meaningful progress toward gender equality in financial literacy and economic participation, which has broad societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: More UK women are investing and earning higher returns than men
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the UK, fewer women invest compared to men. While about 40% of men have investments, only around 25% of women do. This difference comes from long-held cultural habits where men usually made financial decisions for their families.

**What happened** – New research shows women who invest often get better results than men. For example, a study by Fidelity International found women’s investments grew by 50% over three years, while men’s grew by 47%. Experts believe women’s success may come from trading less often, which can help investments grow more steadily.

**Impact** – This shows that when women do invest, they can be very successful. It also points to a positive change in how women are thinking and talking about money. More women are becoming confident in managing their finances, which helps close the gap between men and women in wealth building.

**What's next step** – Women-led groups and experts want to encourage even more women to learn about and join investing. By sharing knowledge and supporting each other, more women could start investing earlier and grow their money over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UK women are investing less often than men but earning higher returns, signaling growing financial confidence and success among women investors.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – De nouvelles recherches montrent que les femmes qui investissent obtiennent souvent de meilleurs résultats que les hommes. Par exemple, une étude de Fidelity International a révélé que les investissements des femmes ont augmenté de 50 % en trois ans, contre 47 % pour les hommes. Les experts pensent que le succès des femmes vient du fait qu’elles négocient moins souvent, ce qui aide leurs investissements à croître plus régulièrement.

**Impact** – Cela montre que lorsque les femmes investissent, elles peuvent réussir. Cela reflète aussi un changement positif dans la manière dont les femmes pensent et parlent d’argent. De plus en plus de femmes gagnent en confiance dans la gestion de leurs finances, ce qui aide à réduire l’écart entre hommes et femmes dans la création de richesse.

**Prochaine étape** – Des groupes dirigés par des femmes et des experts veulent encourager encore plus de femmes à apprendre et à investir. En partageant leurs connaissances et en se soutenant, davantage de femmes pourraient commencer à investir plus tôt et faire croître leur argent.

**Phrase clé** – Au Royaume-Uni, les femmes investissent moins que les hommes mais obtiennent de meilleurs rendements, signe d’une confiance et d’un succès financier croissants chez les femmes investisseurs.
